description: Server Actions are asynchronous functions marked with the 'use server' directive that execute on the server. They are the Next.js-native mechanism for handling form submissions, data mutations, and any server-side logic triggered from the client. Server Actions are invoked from Client Components (via event handlers or form actions) and Server Components (via form actions). They receive FormData or typed arguments, execute server-side, and can revalidate caches, redirect, set cookies, and perform database operations. Server Actions are automatically exposed as POST endpoints by Next.js — they require authentication and authorization validation inside every action.

constraints.title: Every Server Action Must Validate Authentication and Authorization
constraints.problem: Server Actions are automatically exposed as POST endpoints accessible from the internet. Without authentication and authorization checks inside every action, unauthenticated or unauthorized users can invoke them directly.
constraints.whyItMatters: Next.js does not automatically protect Server Actions behind authentication. Layout- or page-level session checks are bypassed when actions are called directly. Every action must be treated as a public API endpoint and independently verify that the caller is authenticated and has permission to perform the requested operation.
forbiddenPatterns: Server Actions with no session or authentication check
Relying on layout.tsx or page.tsx authentication guards to protect Server Action invocations
Relying on middleware authentication alone without per-action checks
Performing database mutations before verifying the user's identity and permission
Trusting client-supplied user IDs without server-side verification
Server Actions that accept an adminFlag from formData without verifying server-side role
allowedPatterns: Calling getSession() or auth() at the top of every Server Action before any mutation
Returning early with an error object if the session is invalid
Verifying that the authenticated user owns the resource being mutated
Using Zod or similar schema validation on all inputs before mutation
Centralizing auth checks in a DAL (Data Access Layer) called by all actions
productionRisks: Unauthorized data mutations by unauthenticated users
architectureImplications: Every Server Action is an implicit API endpoint and must be designed with that security posture
A Data Access Layer (DAL) enforces authorization centrally, reducing per-action boilerplate
Server Actions should perform the minimum mutation necessary and return minimal data
optimizationGuidance: Create an authenticated action wrapper that injects verified session into all actions
Use a DAL that performs authorization checks before any database access
quickFixes: Add const session = await getSession(); if (!session) return { error: 'Unauthorized' }; at the top of every action
architectureSuggestions: Create a createAction(handler) wrapper that enforces authentication, input validation (Zod), and error handling as cross-cutting concerns
Never pass user IDs from the client; always derive the acting user's identity from the server-side session

invalid: async function deletePost(id: string) { 'use server'; await db.post.delete({ where: { id } }) } // No auth check!
valid: async function deletePost(id: string) { 'use server'; const session = await getSession(); if (!session) return { error: 'Unauthorized' }; const post = await db.post.findUnique({ where: { id } }); if (post.authorId !== session.userId) return { error: 'Forbidden' }; await db.post.delete({ where: { id } }); revalidateTag('posts') }

constraints.title: Server Action Arguments and Return Values Must Be Serializable
constraints.problem: Server Actions receive arguments and return values that must cross the server/client boundary via the RSC serialization protocol. Non-serializable types cannot be passed to or returned from Server Actions.
constraints.whyItMatters: The communication channel between client invocation and server execution uses the same serialization protocol as the RSC Payload. Passing or returning class instances, functions, Symbols, or circular references will cause serialization errors at runtime.
forbiddenPatterns: Returning class instances from Server Actions
Returning Error class instances directly (return plain error objects instead)
Passing functions as arguments to Server Actions
Passing class instances as arguments
Returning database model instances (ORM objects) instead of plain DTOs
Returning circular reference objects
allowedPatterns: Returning plain success/error objects: { success: true, data: { id: '...' } } or { error: 'message' }
Receiving FormData (natively serializable for form actions)
Receiving primitive types: strings, numbers, booleans
Receiving plain objects and arrays of serializable values
Using useActionState (React 19) to manage action state in the client
productionRisks: Runtime serialization errors crashing the action invocation
Type errors that only appear at runtime, not at compile time
architectureImplications: Server Actions reinforce DTO boundaries: map database records to plain objects before returning
Error handling should use structured return values, not thrown Error instances, for client-consumable error state
optimizationGuidance: Define explicit TypeScript return type interfaces for all Server Actions
Always map ORM results to plain POJOs before returning from Server Actions
quickFixes: Return { success: true, data: plainObject } instead of the ORM instance
For errors, return { success: false, error: 'message' } instead of throwing
architectureSuggestions: Define ActionResult<T> = { success: true; data: T } | { success: false; error: string } as a standard return type across all Server Actions

invalid: async function createUser(data) { 'use server'; const user = await db.user.create({ data }); return user; // ORM instance, not serializable }
valid: async function createUser(data) { 'use server'; const user = await db.user.create({ data }); return { success: true, data: { id: user.id, name: user.name, email: user.email } } }

constraints.title: Server Actions Must Not Be Used for Read Operations
constraints.problem: Server Actions are semantically and architecturally designed for mutations (writes). Using them for data fetching (reads) is an anti-pattern that bypasses the caching system and adds unnecessary POST request overhead.
constraints.whyItMatters: Server Actions are invoked via POST requests and are never cached. Using a Server Action to fetch data means every read triggers a non-cacheable POST request to the server, eliminating any possibility of data caching, static prerendering, or ISR for that data. Server Components with async/await are the correct tool for server-side reads.
forbiddenPatterns: Using a Server Action to fetch and return data for display in a Client Component
Calling a Server Action on component mount (useEffect) to load initial data
Using Server Actions as a replacement for Route Handlers for GET requests
allowedPatterns: Server Components with async/await for all data reads
Route Handlers (GET) for data that Client Components must fetch dynamically
Server Actions exclusively for: form submissions, database mutations, cache revalidation, redirects, cookie operations
productionRisks: Uncacheable data reads increasing server load
Performance degradation from POST overhead for read operations
architectureImplications: The read/write separation is architecturally significant in Next.js: Server Components handle reads, Server Actions handle writes
This separation enables the caching system to function correctly
optimizationGuidance: Perform all data reads in Server Components; pass data as props to Client Components
Use Route Handlers for truly dynamic client-side reads (user interactions, real-time)
quickFixes: Move the data-fetching logic out of the Server Action and into the parent Server Component
architectureSuggestions: Enforce a naming convention: actions/*.ts for mutations (Server Actions), lib/data/*.ts for reads (called from Server Components)

invalid:
'use client'
import { getUsers } from './actions'
useEffect(() => { getUsers().then(setUsers) }, []) // Anti-pattern: Server Action for reads

constraints.title: Server Actions Must Validate Input with Schema Validation
constraints.problem: Server Actions that accept user input and write to databases without schema validation are vulnerable to unexpected data types, SQL injection (via ORM misuse), and application crashes from malformed input.
constraints.whyItMatters: Client-side validation is easily bypassed. Server Actions receive raw client input that must be treated as untrusted. Without server-side validation, malformed or malicious input can corrupt data, crash the application, or create security vulnerabilities.
forbiddenPatterns: Writing formData.get('field') directly to a database without type coercion or validation
Trusting client-supplied type information
Using parseInt() or parseFloat() without validating the input is actually a number
Accepting user input into database queries without parameterization (ORM misuse)
Skipping validation because client-side validation already exists
allowedPatterns: Using Zod schema.safeParse() or schema.parse() on all action inputs
Using Valibot or similar typed validation libraries
Returning validation errors as structured ActionResult objects for client display
Using FormData with Zod by calling formData.get() inside the schema coercion
productionRisks: Data corruption from unexpected input types
Application crashes from null/undefined access on unvalidated fields
Security vulnerabilities from unvalidated user-supplied data
architectureImplications: Input validation is a mandatory cross-cutting concern for all Server Actions
Validation errors should be returned (not thrown) for graceful client-side display
optimizationGuidance: Define Zod schemas adjacent to their Server Actions for co-location of input contracts
Reuse validation schemas for both client-side and server-side validation
quickFixes: Add const result = schema.safeParse(Object.fromEntries(formData)); if (!result.success) return { errors: result.error.flatten() } at the start of every action
architectureSuggestions: Create a validateInput<T>(schema, data) utility that standardizes validation error responses across all Server Actions

invalid: async function createPost(formData: FormData) { 'use server'; await db.post.create({ data: { title: formData.get('title'), content: formData.get('content') } }) // Unvalidated input directly to DB }
valid:
const schema = z.object({ title: z.string().min(1).max(200), content: z.string().min(10) })
async function createPost(formData: FormData) { 'use server'; const result = schema.safeParse({ title: formData.get('title'), content: formData.get('content') }); if (!result.success) return { errors: result.error.flatten() }; await db.post.create({ data: result.data }); revalidateTag('posts') }

constraints.title: Use Server Actions for Mutations, Not Inline Route Handler Calls
constraints.problem: Using fetch('/api/...') from Client Components to perform mutations that could be handled directly by Server Actions adds unnecessary boilerplate, increases round-trip overhead, and bypasses the cache invalidation integration of Server Actions.
constraints.whyItMatters: Server Actions are invoked via a direct RPC-like mechanism that is more efficient than a full HTTP API call, type-safe through the TypeScript boundary, and automatically integrated with Next.js's revalidation system. Using Route Handlers for mutations that have no external consumer adds needless complexity.
forbiddenPatterns: fetch('/api/update-post', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify(data) }) from a Client Component when a Server Action would suffice
Creating Route Handlers for simple CRUD mutations consumed only by the same Next.js app
Manually calling revalidatePath after a fetch mutation in a Client Component
allowedPatterns: Server Actions for all internal mutations (form submissions, button actions, CRUD operations)
Route Handlers for external API consumers (mobile apps, third-party webhooks, public APIs)
Route Handlers for streaming responses or SSE
Route Handlers for GET requests that must be publicly accessible as API endpoints
productionRisks: Unnecessary API boilerplate that must be maintained
Cache invalidation must be manually triggered from Route Handlers (does not clear Router Cache automatically)
Type safety lost across the HTTP boundary
architectureImplications: Route Handlers are for external API consumers; Server Actions are for internal UI mutations
Server Actions provide type safety across the server/client boundary that Route Handlers cannot
optimizationGuidance: Replace internal fetch-to-API mutations with Server Actions
Maintain Route Handlers only for endpoints that have or will have external consumers
quickFixes: Convert the mutation logic from a Route Handler into a Server Action and call it directly from the form or Client Component event handler
architectureSuggestions: Establish a rule: Route Handlers are public API surface; Server Actions are internal mutations. Document the distinction in the project's architecture decision records.

invalid:
'use client'
async function handleSubmit(data) { await fetch('/api/create-post', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify(data) }); router.refresh() }
